title: Right View and the Three Doors of Liberation
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up Right View, the first factor of the Noble Eightfold Path, through the Three Doors of Liberation: emptiness, signlessness, and aimlessness. For emptiness, IkuShun draws on Thich Nhat Hanh's teaching that a self is made of non-self elements, and on watching IkuShun's son grow up as a reminder that nothing stays in one form. For signlessness, IkuShun describes how a dandelion becomes a weed in the mind, and how an overheard complaint in a restaurant about a Prius blocking a horse trailer reveals the complainer's views. Aimlessness loosens the pull of status and wealth, and IkuShun closes on the word transparency: seeing through concepts a little more clearly while still living among them.

sentences.text: *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect Dharma is rarely met within a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Can everybody hear me okay?
Well, thank you all for being here this morning.
Today's talk I titled Right View.
I'm going to talk again about Right View, as Edie did last week.
So I named it Right View and the Three Doors of Liberation.
Thank you for joining me again.
I think I'm going to call this talk a little garment.
It's short, as Gil Fronsdale calls them, but we'll have plenty of time for group discussion after.
I also want to talk a little bit about Right View, the first of the subjects in the Noble Eightfold Path laid out by the Buddha.
While there is no real order to the facets of the path, because they are totally interconnected, I really feel like Right View is a fundamental ground on which the others can spring forth.
Right View doesn't mean correct view, as we know.
It doesn't mean right in the sense of good or bad or moral or immoral.
It means to have a clear view of how things are at a deeper level than our thoughts about the world, deeper than our imaginings and deeper than our habit perceptions and concepts.
It's important to understand the truths of existence, the Three Dharma Seals of impermanence, no separate self, and reality deeper than notions and ideas.
Some of the deepest offerings of the Buddha include these Three Dharma Seals, also called the Three Marks of Existence.
The Buddha also taught about the Three Doors of Liberation.
For me, all of these tools help me bring awareness to the characteristics of my humanness, my perceptions, my concepts, my picking and choosing, and be able to see another dimension at the same time.
They allow me to bring a transparency to the way I see the world.
They offer an alternate view to the one that I may be used to, and a way of holding two truths at the same time.
So what are these Three Doors of Liberation?
They are emptiness, signlessness, and aimlessness.
We'll take a look at these and examine how they offer guidance on Right View.
We speak about emptiness a lot, and as Edie was saying in her talk recently, that word can bring a lot of confusion.
Emptiness, empty: empty of what?
Empty of a separate self.
As my root teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, always said, if something is empty of one thing, it's full of something else.
In his explanation, if something is empty of a separate individual self, it's full of everything else.
When we look deeply, we see that we are everything: our parents, the sun, calcium from the stars, nutrients from the earth.
This is not a theory.
This is reality.
Thich Nhat Hanh would often say that a self is made of all non-self elements.
This is the nature of reality, the great manifestation of everything, and it's always changing.

Even though I'm living in a world of self and other, of things that appear to have separate entities, I can also train myself to recognize this other truth, the truth of no separate self and inner being.
As I'm functioning in this world as an individual, I can recognize the self that is made of non-self elements.
I can see how the food I just ate is assimilated into me.
I can often note my mother's gestures through me, or my father's way of speaking through me.
Another facet of emptiness is that nothing is permanent and nothing continues in the same form.
It's wonderful for me to remember this as I'm grasping onto something in this moment.
Everything changes.
If it's something that I don't like, I realize it won't last forever, like political, whatever.
But if it's something that I love, I need to appreciate it for its fleeting existence.
So often as parents, we think of a time in a child's life that we wanted to last forever.
But if that were the case, how could he or she grow up to become an adult?
I think of my son and how I used to love each stage of his development, but now I'm seeing him as a young adult, so passionate about his music and his life of music.
What if he stayed a young child forever, before this love even developed or blossomed?
I know that he will grow older, life will change, the world will change, I will change.
And at some point, I won't even be here anymore.
So I try to remember those things and soak up the wonder of what is right now.
What is he doing in this present time?
What am I doing?
It's a comfort for me to see his growing up, his living and his dying and all those things.
Sometimes they aren't any different from anything else in this great mysterious unfolding.
And sometimes we think about that.
We think of our parents or our children or ourselves and we think, oh gosh, I too am going to die.
But for me, it's a comfort knowing that all things are like that.
It isn't anything different or special.
Everything goes through that.
So I think the ability to see the impermanent nature and the interconnected nature of things is so important.
There's a balance that we maintain around right perspective, right view.
Everything comes and goes.
There can be a deep grief when something is lost or someone we love dies.
Thich Nhat Hanh talked about his grief for the loss of his mother until he really deeply penetrated the truth that she is everywhere and present in everything.
This is the truth of inner being.
I've often struggled and felt the need to act in a moment when I see another life that's suffering.
I try to have an appropriate response.
For instance, I used to feel compelled to move all the worms off of the sidewalk after it rained.
How did I even know that this was beneficial?
And how could I have ever done that anyway?
This is a perception in my mind.
There's a balance in knowing that it's all right to grieve and care for something, and to recognize that we can't save things in that way of moving the worms.
That's not right view.
Everything is constantly being born and constantly dying, constantly changing form.
And yet on a deeper level, everything is still here.
This doesn't mean that we shouldn't take action as appropriate, but it does mean that we need to hold things with clear understanding.
Thich Nhat Hanh reminds us that every cell in our body is in flux, coming into existence and dying and going away.
I remember reading something where he said that we can't organize a funeral for every cell in our body.
So it's that balance in recognizing that, and in the midst of that, still being okay, still having the ability to have compassion and to grieve and love the things that we love.
For me, a continuing part of my practice is how to respond in each moment with each different circumstance.
I think having right view is a ground for having an appropriate response.
The second door of liberation is called signlessness.
What does that mean?
Signs here mean to have an appearance, to be an object of our perception.
When we see an object, our mind may instantly attach a label to it.
When we see a dandelion flower, we may think, oh, it's a weed, instantly.
And then we may go on to give ourselves an opportunity for action, like, oh, I need to pull it.
Signs are instruments that we use constantly, and some of them are useful, but they're not the absolute truth.
The flower in our minds, in our society: flower, dandelion, weed.
Those are all concepts.
Those are all ideas, labels that we've given to something.
But that's not the reality of the existence of that thing.
Often they're not the absolute truth, and often they can be deceptive.
The Diamond Sutra says, wherever there's a sign, there's a deception.
There's an illusion.
Perceptions can also tell us a lot about the perceiver as well as the object of the perception.
An example that I thought of, probably more pertinent a few years ago than now, is the cars that we choose.
If we owned a Prius, for instance, we may have chosen in our mind that this is a symbol of environmental stewardship.
But this perception could have contained also some aloofness or some pride about owning the Prius, being in the club, maybe similar to how we are with our Subarus right now.
But somebody else might see my car and immediately perceive snobbiness, or a perception of being liberal, or maybe even not caring about American jobs.
These are all perceptions that we have.
I was in a restaurant a few years ago overhearing someone complaining about somebody else parked at the trailhead in such a way that she couldn't get her truck and her horse trailer turned around.
But she had to know it was a Prius, of course.
So this immediately revealed to me her views and the conditions in her life that led to those perceptions.
And we all have them.
I have perceptions when I see big black diesel trucks coming at me in the same way.
We also see how much marketing preys on perceptions, like anti-aging, anti-wrinkle cream, or expensive gadgets, or even opportunities for trips to the moon.
These are all preying on our perceptions of things.
We hold some of these labels and views more strongly than others.
There are blatantly obvious signs and some innocuous signs that help the community to flow more smoothly.
So they're not all deceptive.
They're not all illusions.
They can be functional, of course, in our society where we live.
But some of them are more subtle.
I remember when I was young, I was always annoyed by the sign up the canyon in Colorado that said "Land of Many Uses."
For others, it was a positive sign, a land that was useful.
But for me, it reflected our societal view that we don't value things for what they are, only if they're useful for us in some way.
Either way, it's good to recognize all of this: to recognize the elements in me that are influenced by what and how I influence, and how I see the world.
I can see the influence of other ancestors in me in the same way, physically, but also in the mental energies that I have.
I can recognize concepts and ideas, perhaps a piece of racism, perhaps an eccentric notion.
I can see communal and societal influences as they arise.
I can recognize a conflict that I had between my dad and his frontiersman views versus my liberal ways growing up in Boulder in the 70s.
Sometimes the notions can be really subtle, but with practice of awareness and mindfulness, I can detect them more easily.
Why is this beneficial?
I think it helps us understand why we do what we do, and it helps touch the truth of who I am.
Dogen says to study the self is to let go of the self, and to let go of the self is to be informed by a myriad of things.
Without this awareness of our intellectual thoughts and perceptions, we're unable to see that deeper truth: the truth of impermanence, no separate self, existence beyond notions and ideas.
This awareness helps me to see the truth of a lack of independent identity.
It doesn't mean that we're not also independent and separate, living and functioning in this relative dimension.
But along with that is the absolute world, the world that Thich Nhat Hanh called the ultimate dimension.
We're not trying to get rid of this relative world that we live in and function in.
But we also want to recognize and hold both.
Form is emptiness, emptiness is form.
The last of the three doors of liberation is aimlessness, or wishlessness.
It means that there's nothing that we need to put in front of ourselves and chase after.
We can allow things to just be, including ourselves.
Recognizing that we don't need to run or to strive or to struggle is freedom.
Just to be is enough.
If we truly believe that we are already Buddhas, we can take this time to just experience nowhere to go, nothing to do.
This aimlessness also helps with right view because we're not pulled by signs of power or achieving wealth or status.
We're more able to see through the signs that our society and our world have placed in our heads as things that we need to have for self-worth or self-value.
As I was writing this, I discovered that I like this word transparency, because these tools that I'm talking about, like I said, are not tools to get rid of things.
They're just a way of having this transparency in terms of our notions and ideas and concepts and perceptions.
It's just an ability to see through them a little more, so that we can start realizing that they are not solid.
They're not anything set in stone.
They're not any absolute truth.
The transparency of these perceptions is really beneficial, I think, in recognizing things for what they are.
They can still help us.
They can still come up.
But we can see through them a little more clearly.
They can help release that notion that they're forever, that they're right.
So this awareness gives better clarity, I think, to develop this right view, using these tools to go through recognizing, being aware of things as we go along.
And I think it gives us a clear understanding of ourselves, where we can hold everything together and also feel that deeper existence.
So anyway, that's my talk for today.
I hope we can just open it up for group discussion now.
Well, let me end this, see if I remember.
*May our intentions equally extend to all beings in place with the true merit of the Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dark gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
Thanks, everybody.
